Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is a gastrointestinal motility disorder that results from the reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus or oral cavity resulting in symptoms or complications. The typical symptoms of GERD are heartburn and regurgitation of gastric contents into the oropharynx. GERD affects quality of life and may cause erosive esophagitis, esophageal strictures, and Barrett esophagus, a precursor to esophageal adenocarcinoma. GERD is a clinical diagnosis and is most effectively treated with proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs). Long-term use of PPIs is associated with bone fractures, chronic renal disease, acute renal disease, community-acquired pneumonia, and Clostridium difficile intestinal infection.

Gastroesophageal reflux (GER) in children is very common and refers to the involuntary passage of gastric contents into the esophagus. This is often physiological and managed conservatively. In contrast, GER disease (GERD) is a less common pathologic process causing troublesome symptoms, which may need medical management. Apart from abnormal transient relaxations of the lower esophageal sphincter, other factors that play a role in the pathogenesis of GERD include defects in esophageal mucosal defense, impaired esophageal and gastric motility and clearance, as well as anatomical defects of the lower esophageal reflux barrier such as hiatal hernia. The clinical manifestations of GERD in young children are varied and nonspecific prompting the necessity for careful diagnostic evaluation. Management should be targeted to the underlying aetiopathogenesis and to limit complications of GERD. The following review focuses on up-to-date information regarding of the pathogenesis, diagnostic evaluation and management of GERD in children.

Symptoms potentially attributable to gastroesophageal reflux disease are among those most commonly reported to primary care providers in the outpatient setting. In this review, we discuss clinical approaches to the evaluation and management of these symptoms, including proton pump inhibitor trials as well as specific indications or clinical settings that warrant referral to Gastroenterology specialists.

data.narrative: The typical symptoms of GERD are heartburn and regurgitation of stomach contents into the throat [18#0]. The condition happens when stomach contents flow back into the esophagus or mouth, and it can damage the esophagus over time [18#1]. If left untreated, GERD can lead to serious problems including inflammation, narrowing of the esophagus, and a condition called Barrett esophagus, which can develop into esophageal cancer [18#2]. In children, the symptoms are varied and not specific, which makes diagnosis harder [19#3]. In children, ordinary reflux is common and usually harmless, while GERD is a less common but more serious problem that may need treatment [19#4][19#5]. In children, risk factors include abnormal relaxation of the valve between the stomach and esophagus, weakness in the esophageal lining, poor movement and emptying of the esophagus and stomach, and physical defects such as hiatal hernia [19#6]. Reflux symptoms are among the most common reasons people visit their primary care doctor [20#7]. Long-term use of the main medications used to treat GERD, called proton-pump inhibitors, can carry risks including bone fractures, kidney disease, pneumonia, and intestinal infection [18#8]. In adults, reflux symptoms are typically evaluated with proton pump inhibitor trials, and certain situations call for referral to a gastroenterology specialist [20#9]. The medical concept is recorded under the name Gastroesophageal reflux (GERD) in MedGen [2]. Related literature also uses the entity name Gastroesophageal Reflux [3]. Several published articles are titled Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease [1][6][9][15]. One publication focuses on what is new in childhood GERD and is titled Gastroesophageal reflux disease in children: What's new right now [12]. A set of PubMed articles are identified by their record numbers: PMID 29132520 [5], PMID 33351044 [8], PMID 36170502 [11], PMID 37034973 [14], and PMID 37516506 [17]. Clinical trials are studying treatments including famotidine for non-erosive GERD [4], pantoprazole for adults with acid reflux symptoms [7], the natural history of reflux in children and adolescents [10], on-demand treatment of reflux disease [13], and endoscopic fundoplication as a placebo-controlled procedure [16].
